name: Femi Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Femi. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a framing and roofing carpenter for a housebuilder doing a new estate called Millbrook Fields, about 140 family houses on the edge of town. On a good day my gang of four frames the walls on two plots and gets the roof trusses up on another. I start at 7:30, and by eleven I've usually been up and down the scaffold twenty times. I like seeing a house go from slab to roof in a fortnight; what wears me out is the rain and the plots where the brickies are behind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and who's on your gang?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eight years, since my trade certificate. My gang is Mo, who leads it, me, and two younger ones, Lewis and Kofi, who are both decent now. The firm's been steady, builds about 400 houses a year, and they pay above the going rate to keep good framers.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Clara, who's an accountant at a mid-sized firm in town, doing small business accounts and tax returns. We rent, but we've got about eight months of costs saved and some money in an index fund, which is Clara's doing. I do the odd decking or pergola job on weekends, and I've used one of those AI chat apps now and then to write the quotes properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought: useful for writing a quote for a decking job, not much else. People were saying the robots were coming for houses, and they're not. I'd probably make a joke about it on the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay pretty good for us. Housing's always needed, my firm's busy, and Clara's job is safe too. The only thing on my mind would be the deposit for a house, which we've been chasing for two years with prices going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep framing at Millbrook and whatever estate comes next. Keep putting about six hundred a month into the house deposit. I'd keep doing two or three weekend jobs a month and use the AI app for the quotes like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A little impatient about the house, but that's not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the house deposit situation, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got the eight months of costs set aside, and the deposit fund on top is about half of what we need for a three-bed on Station Road. If prices keep going up at the rate they have, it's another two years. Clara has a spreadsheet; I just transfer the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything at work that bothers you already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm went through a slow patch a few years back when interest rates went up, and they cut the subbies first. We full-timers were fine. But you remember stuff like that.

say: I'd say AI is useful for **writing quotes**, not much else.
I'd joke on the group chat that **robots** never came for house building.
think: Things stay good: **housing demand** is steady and his partner Clara's job is safe.
His main pressure is the **house deposit** as prices keep rising.
do: Keep **framing** at Millbrook and the next estate.
Keep saving about **six hundred** a month for the deposit.
Keep doing **weekend jobs** and writing quotes with the AI app.
feel: **Calm**, with some impatience about buying a house.
S0.quote: People were saying the robots were coming for houses, and they're not.
fieldNote: His only live pressure is the **deposit**, not his job.
He remembers the **rate-rise slowdown** but felt secure as a full-timer.
His partner manages the **household money**, which he's happy to admit.

steps.text: Keep framing houses at Millbrook Fields with the same gang
Put six hundred a month toward a three-bed house deposit
Keep doing weekend decking jobs with AI-written quotes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say framers are fine but the office people need to watch out. At work I'd say the site managers will spend more time on tablets and less shouting, which would be nice. With friends I'd be careful, because Clara's work is right in the firing line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes for a while; framing is hands on. But Clara does tax returns and small business accounts, and that's exactly the checking and planning stuff this takes over. If her firm needs half the staff, that's our deposit plan in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Clara to get ahead and learn the new accounting software properly, and I'd back her if she wanted to do a course. We'd keep saving but maybe slow the house hunt for a year until we see how her firm goes. I'd start using the AI app more for my side jobs too, invoices and ordering materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. My own job feels fine, but it's like watching someone else's car skid on ice and you're the passenger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Clara, that first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not in a hurry and she shouldn't panic about the house. I'd say my pay's steady and we can live on it for a while if we have to. Then I'd probably go quiet and do the maths in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If her firm cut staff, could you make up the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. I could take more weekend jobs and maybe go up to overtime on the estate. But I'm not doing seven days for long, my back wouldn't take it.

I'd be careful with friends because his partner's **accounting job** is exposed.
think: His own **framing work** barely changes for years.
Clara's **tax and accounts** work is exactly what this picture takes over.
If her firm halves staff, their **house plan** is in trouble.
do: Encourage Clara to **learn the new software** or take a course.
Slow the **house hunt** for a year while still saving.
Use the AI app more for **invoices and ordering** on side jobs.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a passenger watching someone else's car skid.
S1.quote: My own job feels fine, but it's like watching someone else's car skid on ice and you're the passenger.
fieldNote: His worry is the **household's second income**, not his own.
He's realistic about **overtime limits** and his back.
He'd offer reassurance aloud and **do the maths** quietly.

steps.text: Back Clara to take a course in the new accounting software
Pause house viewings for a year while still saving monthly
Use the AI app for invoices and ordering on weekend jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to be ready and the government needs a plan, fast. At work I'd say the robots aren't here yet so let's keep working. But I'd be quieter than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Clara's job probably goes in 2028 or near it, and mine goes around 2031, when I'm 32. That's both of us within three years. Our savings and the index fund would carry us a while, but forever is a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, forget buying the house; we'd keep renting and keep the deposit as a survival fund, which with the index fund is well over a year. I'd ask the firm if there's any route into running or setting up the robot framing rigs, since I know framing. And Clara and I would cut the extras, no holiday, cheaper car insurance, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. For the first time I'd be properly worried about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the deposit becomes a survival fund. How long does that last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Clara's out of work and I'm still framing, a long time, years even. If we're both out, maybe eighteen months, two years if we're careful. That's the number I'd have in my head all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mo and the younger lads on the gang?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lewis and Kofi to get some kind of second skill now, while they're young. Mo is older, he's 50, so he might just about make it to an early retirement. I'd tell Mo nothing; he'd already know.

say: I'd say the **government** needs a plan fast.
At work I'd say **keep working** because robots aren't here yet.
think: His partner's job likely goes around **2028**, and his framing by **2031**.
Both **household incomes** could go within three years.
do: Drop the **house purchase** and turn the deposit into a survival fund.
Ask the firm about running **robot framing rigs**.
Cut extras like the **holiday** and car insurance costs.
feel: **Alarmed**, properly worried about money for the first time.
S2.quote: If we're both out, maybe eighteen months, two years if we're careful. That's the number I'd have in my head all the time.
fieldNote: The **double exposure** of his household drives his mood more than his own job.
His public line stays **steady** while he privately counts months.
He thinks of **younger colleagues** first when asked about others.

steps.text: Drop the house purchase and keep the deposit as a survival fund
Ask the housebuilder about jobs running robot framing rigs
Cut the summer holiday and shop around for cheaper car insurance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to get ready and people should use them. I'd mention it to the gang but not make a big deal. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clara gets hit in 2031 and me around 2034, when I'm 35. That's a few more years to earn and save. I'd say it's worrying but we'd have time for at least one of us to land somewhere safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go for the house, but cheaper, maybe a two-bed instead of three, so the mortgage is small. I'd do a short course on site supervision in the next couple of years, because someone has to manage these robot crews. Clara would look at moving from accounts to something like financial advice where people still want a face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's like knowing the shift's going to be long, you just pace yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still buy a house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because renting for forty years with no job is worse than owning something small. If we buy a cheap two-bed now and pay it down hard, at least the roof is ours by the time the robots turn up. Clara's spreadsheet would decide in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving somewhere else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Our families are here and there's plenty of building work locally. If anywhere has jobs left, it'll be here, where they're still building estates.

say: I'd say people should use the **few years** to prepare.
I'd mention it to the gang but **stay out of it** online.
think: His partner's job goes in **2031** and his around **2034**.
There's time for one of them to land somewhere **safer**.
do: Buy a cheaper **two-bed** and pay the mortgage down hard.
Take a short **site supervision** course in the next two years.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, pacing himself like a long shift.
S3.quote: If we buy a cheap two-bed now and pay it down hard, at least the roof is ours by the time the robots turn up.
fieldNote: Extra years turn his plan from **survival** to preparation.
He sees **owning a home** as protection against future job loss.
He stays rooted locally because **building work** is plentiful here.

steps.text: Buy a two-bed instead of a three-bed and overpay the mortgage
Take a short site supervision course within two years
Support Clara moving from accounts into financial advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort ourselves out if we're sensible. Most people at work would say the same. I'd tell friends to start thinking about it, but not to lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm 37 when Clara's side changes and 40 when it's my turn. That's a full run at the house, maybe kids, and building up savings. I'd still be a bit uneasy because Clara's job is the more exposed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy the three-bed on Station Road like we planned, and keep a good buffer. I'd learn the AI tools on site as they come in, not before. Around 2030 I'd start a supervision course, so I'm ready to manage when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It feels like a problem for my late thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this picture change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We'd still have them in the next few years. I'd just want the house paid down faster so we're not stretched when things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first sign you'd be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the firm starts using AI to plan the plots and order trusses without the site office, I've got about three years before the hands-on side follows. That's the sign I'd watch.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if people are sensible.
I'd tell friends to start **thinking about it** without losing sleep.
think: He'd be **37** when his partner's work changes and **40** when his does.
Clara's job is the **more exposed** one, which keeps him uneasy.
do: Buy the **three-bed** on Station Road as planned.
Learn the **AI tools** on site as they arrive.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, seeing it as a problem for later.
S4.quote: When the firm starts using AI to plan the plots and order trusses without the site office, I've got about three years before the hands-on side follows.
fieldNote: He clearly understands the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots.
Family plans, including **children**, go ahead here.
His steady style shows: learn tools **when they arrive**, not before.

steps.text: Buy the three-bed house on Station Road as planned
Learn the site AI planning tools as the firm brings them in
Start a site supervision course around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both me and Clara would be hit within three years, and the savings only go so far. What would help is proper support while people retrain, like a wage while you learn, and the firm giving us first chance at the robot jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about households. Everyone asks about one job, but it's two incomes that pay for a house. A framer married to an accountant is going to get hit twice.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about one job, but it's two incomes that pay for a house. A framer married to an accountant is going to get hit twice.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old framing carpenter** on a 140-house estate, steady and well paid.
He rents with his partner **Clara, an accountant**, and they're saving hard for a house deposit.
He's **calm** about AI Plateau but uneasy in Steady Disruption because Clara's job is exposed.
AGI by 2028 leaves him **alarmed** about both incomes going within three years.
With more warning he'd **buy a home**, take a supervision course and pace changes sensibly.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and his partner would both lose income within three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage while retraining** and first chance at robot jobs from the firm.
